sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
In the global low -carbon transition of power systems with high renewable energy 
integration, pumped-storage has emerged as a core strategic resource for enhancing grid 
resilience, with global plans targeting capacity expansions of tens of gigawatts [1–3]. 
However, systematic planning challenges remain,  including disjointed site selection and 
transmission-corridor planning, the lack of explicit quantification of the resilience value 
of pumped storage in black -start scenarios [4], and the coarse handling of hierarchical 
constraints, including connectivity, N -1 connectivity, and power flow security. Current

planning methods face challenges in balancing computational efficiency with solution 
quality [5 ,6]. Therefore, developing a bi -objective resilient backbone -grid planning ap-
proach that simultaneously integrates economic performance and system resilience, in-
corporates precise N-1 connectivity analysis, and fully exploits the pumped storage hub 
effect is of significant theoretical and engineering importance [7,8]. 
Current research on pumped-storage and backbone-grid-coordinated planning pri-
marily focuses on economic and technical feasibility, while paying insufficient attention 
to the resilience-support value of pumped-storage under extreme conditions [9,10]. Exist-
ing studies on resilience value modeling predominantly focus on the functional imple-
mentation of pumped -storage equipment. Although resilience -support pathways for 
pumped-storage systems have been discussed from  perspectives such as black-start con-
trol, emergency output regulation, and rapid load response, quantitative models that ex-
plicitly characterize the contribution of pumped -storage units during post -fault system 
recovery are still lacking . This results in insufficient support for differentiated resilience 
evaluation of planning schemes and complicates the accurate assessment of the unique 
resilience value of pumped -storage resources [11–13]. Regarding N -1 connectivity con-
straints, traditional methods have significant limitations: optimization approache s using 
penalty functions or slack coefficient meth ods for N -1 overload expectations are essen-
tially soft constraint designs. These methods cannot strictly satisfy the rigid safety require-
ment of edge connectivity ≥2, and in complex network topologies, they tend to generate 
numerous infeasible solutions, c onsuming excessive computational resources [14–16], 
thereby reducing planning efficiency. Meanwhile, few studies addressing rigid con-
straints encounter issues such as exponential computational complexity and convergence 
difficulties, making them unsuitable for large -scale backbone-grid planning scenarios. In 
developing evaluation metrics for planning, existing models primarily prioritize eco-
nomic viability and resource compatibility. While current pumped -storage site selection 
frameworks incorporate multiple indicators, such as investment costs, output capacity 
alignment, and environmental benefits, they systematically exclude the resilience dimen-
sion. This oversight leads to planning outcomes that fail to  adequately address both sys-
tem resilience under extreme conditions and recovery efficiency [17–21]. The critical gap 
in this field lies in explicitly quantifying the resilience value of pumped storage, precisely 
satisfying the stringent N-1 connectivity requirements, and fully integrating resilience as-
sessment into planning models [22]. 
This study addresses the identified research gaps by investigating both the planning 
model and intelligent optimization algorithm levels. At the model level, with pumped 
storage serving as the core power source for system black start, the resilience evaluation 
system incorporates restoration -distance contribution and capacity -weighted between-
ness centrality . A dual -objective “economy-resilience” planning model is constructed, 
with connectivity, N-1 connectivity (edge connectivity ≥ 2), and dual-scenario power flow 
security of pumped-storage units as rigid constraints. At the algorithm level, a bi-objective 
three-stage evolutionary algorithm, TER-NSGA-II, is proposed within the computational 
intelligence framework. The optimization process is divided into three phases: connectiv-
ity construction, N-1 connectivity reinforcement, and safety convergence. During the con-
nectivity reinforcement phase, edge connectivity is precisely validated using the maxi-
mum flow-minimum cut theorem. Simulation results from the IEEE  118-bus system, to-
gether with extended validation on the IEEE 300 -bus system, demonstrate the effective-
ness of the proposed method in terms of optimization accuracy, solution-set quality, and 
engineering applicability. 
It should be noted that this study adopts a deterministic modeling framework to rep-
resent typical operating scenarios and does not explicitly account for renewable genera-
tion variability or load uncertainty. Existing studies have shown that uncertainty can

significantly affect the capacity configuration and operation results of power and inte-
grated energy systems [23,24]. In addition, DC power flow is employed to improve com-
putational efficiency at the planning stage, while voltage magnitude constraints, reactive 
power effects, and network losses are not explicitly modeled. Therefore, the results of this 
study are more sui table for candidate backbone -grid screening at the planning stage ra-
ther than for detailed operational validation. These limitations are further discussed in the 
model description and conclusion sections, together with possible directions for future 
extension.

sections.title: 2 Resilient Backbone-Grid and Pumped-Storage Resilience Value
2.1 The Connotation and Construction Criteria of the Resilient Backbone Grid
sections.text:
In extreme disaster scenarios, a resilient backbone  grid is a core network structure 
designed to ensure continuous power supply to critical loads, formed by optimized trans-
mission channels with topological redundancy and rapid recovery capabilities [2 5,26]. 
When pumped-storage systems are extensively integrated as black -start power sources, 
elevating them to “resilient cores,” their hub locations and bidirectional power support 
capacities must be incorporated into planning [27]. 
The resilient backbone-grid framework under study is defined as follows: given fixed 
pumped-storage connection locations and capacities, the resilient backbone grid is con-
structed through optimized backbone-channel selection under hard constraints of connec-
tivity, N-1 connectivity (edge connectivity ≥ 2), and dual-scenario pumped-storage power 
flow security, while resilience is quantified by recovery -distance contribution and capac-
ity-weighted betweenness centrality. The construction process follows four fundamental 
principles, which are systematically incorporated into the subsequent model: 
a. Bidirectional power-carrying criterion: The grid structure must satisfy transmission 
capacity constraints under both pumped-storage power generation and pumping op-
eration modes, ensuring bidirectional power flow security and balance.  
b. N-1 connectivity criterion: At least two edge-disjoint paths must exist between core-
load buses and pumped -storage black -start power sources, ensuring a minimum 
edge connectivity of two to maintain power supply continuity during single compo-
nent failures. 
c. Power supply assurance criterion: It must cover all critical power buses, core -load 
buses, and black-start buses (e.g., pumped-storage plants) to ensure physical connec-
tivity of essential services under extreme conditions. 
d. Economic-resilience synergy principle: Under strict compliance with the aforemen-
tioned safety hard constraints, grid planning should balance construction costs with 
resilience benefits, offering diversified solutions ranging from economic priority to 
safety priority.

sections.title: 2.2 Technical Characteristics and Recovery Value of Pumped-Storage Plants
sections.text:
As a strategic resource for enhancing the safety and resilience of power systems, 
pumped-storage plants feature bidirectional power flow ( generation and pumping ), mi-
nute-level response capabilities, and black -start functionality [2 8]. For fixed -speed 
pumped-storage units, the pumping power 𝑃𝑝𝑢𝑚𝑝  is typically represented at the rated 
power 𝑃𝑁 [29], whereas the generation power 𝑃𝑔𝑒𝑛 is allowed to vary within a practical 
range of 50–100% of 𝑃𝑁 [30].

This study integrates pumped storage into the black-start power supply pool for con-
nectivity and N -1 connectivity verification. Typically connected to critical grid sections, 
these facilities exhibit high betweenness centrality at grid buses. Their strategic location 
enables efficient power distribution during system recovery. This hub value is quantified 
through recovery -distance contribution and capacity -weighted betweenness centrality , 
thereby incorporating the technical characteristics of pumped storage  into the resilience 
objective and mapping them to system-level resilience gains.

sections.title: 3.1 Quantitative Framework for Resilience Recovery
sections.text:
Grid resilience emphasizes maintaining critical services under extreme disturbances, 
differing from traditional reliability, with a focus on post-disturbance recovery speed and 
continuity of system functionality [31,32]. Existing studies have shown that power system 
resilience assessment usually needs to consider both structural and functional changes, 
since a single performance perspective is insufficient to fully characterize the system state 
after disturbances [33].  Similarly, comprehensive resilience as sessment frameworks also 
emphasize constructing integrated indicators from multiple dimensions to improve the 
overall characterization of system states [3 4]. This study focuses on post -disaster scenar-
ios, quantifying the backbone grid ’s power supply reconstruction capacity for core loads 
supported by pumped-storage black-start systems. This capacity depends on two factors: 
first, the electrical accessibility of recovery paths, referring to the electrical distance be-
tween core loads and black-start power sources; second, the hubness of pumped -storage 
networks, indicating their central role in the grid topology. By coupling recovery-distance 
contribution with capacity-weighted betweenness centrality, this paper constructs a sys-
tem resilience mismatch index (𝐹2), where lower values indicate better system resilience.

sections.title: 3.4 System Resilience Mismatch Index
sections.text:
The recovery distance factor and the pumped -storage hub effect factor are coupled 
through a product model. Similarly, comprehensive resilience assessment studies empha-
size the coordinated integration of structural and functional indicators to improve the 
overall characterization of system -state changes [33,34]. Accordingly, the system resili-
ence mismatch index is defined as: 
𝐹2 = 𝐹2,dist × (1 − 𝛼 ⋅ 𝐵𝐶psh) (8) 
where 𝛼 = 0.3 is the hub effect influence coefficient. A smaller value of 𝐹2 indicates a 
stronger ability of the system to maintain power supply to core loads after disturbances 
and therefore reflects better resilience. The product form reflects that restoration distance 
represents the baseline structural difficulty of post -disturbance recovery, whereas the 
pumped-storage hub effect acts as a proportional correction term that captures the en-
hancement introduced by topological centrality and available support capacity. 
The hub effect influence coefficient 𝛼  is introduced to regulate the correction 
strength of the pumped-storage hub effect on the restoration distance. In this study, 𝛼 is 
set to 0.3, which reflects the positive contribution of pumped -storage hub support to sys-
tem recovery while avoiding over -amplification of a single topological attribute, thereby 
preserving engineering interpretability and numerical stability.

ters, and pumped-storage capacities, they remain constant with respect to 𝛼 under a fixed

sections.title: 5 Integration of Three-Stage Framework and Graph-Theoretic
sections.text:
Validation in TER-NSGA-II Algorithm 
The construction of the backbone grid is a high -dimensional, discrete, and highly 
constrained multi-objective combinatorial optimization problem. Traditional mathemati-
cal programming methods are limited by combinatorial explosion and nonlinear con-
straints, making them inefficient for solving such problems. The standard NSGA-II algo-
rithm performs well in general multi-objective optimization due to its elite retention, fast 
non-dominated sorting, and crowding distance mechanism [38]. However, it exhibits in-
sufficient constraint handling capabilities when applied to engineering problems with 
strong constraints [39]. Firstly, the randomness of crossover and mutation often generates 
infeasible solutions that violate connectivity and N -1 connectivity constraints, and reli-
ance on penalty functions severely reduces optimization efficiency. Secondly, it lacks pre-
cise quantification and evolutionary guidance for N -1 connectivity. Finally, it is prone to 
local optima and has difficulty maintaining population diversity, and its fixed elite-selec-
tion mechanism cannot meet the incremental needs of hierarchical constraints [40]. To ad-
dress these issues, this paper proposes a three-stage evolutionary reverse-learning NSGA-
II (TER-NSGA-II), which integrates a three -stage framework and graph -theoretic valida-
tion.

sections.title: 5.1 Three-Stage Iteration and Elite Selection Integrated Framework
sections.text:
The total number of iterations 𝑇𝑚𝑎𝑥 is divided into three stages to match the engi-
neering logic of “first connectivity, then redundancy, and finally safety”:  
a. Stage I (Connectivity Construction): Prioritize retaining individuals with the lowest 
constraint violation values, rapidly converging toward the feasible domain.  
b. Stage II (N-1 Connectivity Reinforcement): This stage balances N-1 connectivity and 
the system resilience mismatch index 𝐹2, giving individuals that satisfy N-1 connec-
tivity a selection advantage. Those that do not satisfy the constraint are identified for 
reinforcement through the minimum cut set, and such edges are favored in genetic 
operations. 
c. Stage III (Convergence and Safety Optimization): Once the population  has largely 
satisfied all hard constraints, the focus shifts to objective optimization and the reten-
tion of Pareto-front individuals. 
The top 5 elite individuals from each generation directly enter the next generation, 
ensuring the stable transmission of high-quality solutions. 
To enhance the interpretability of the staged search process and the transferability of 
parameter settings, the three parameters 𝑇1, 𝑇2, and 𝑇𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑒 are defined as the switching 
generations between Stage I and Stage II, between Stage II and Stage III, and the triggering 
interval of periodic reverse learning, respectively. These parameters jointly determine 
how search effort is allocated across the diff erent stages. Considering their scale depend-
ence on the total number of generations, an automatic configuration procedure based on 
irace is adopted in the case study section to determine their final values [41].

sections.title: 5.2 Hierarchical Constraint Screening Strategy
sections.text:
Rather than relying on the conventional “generate-repair” mode, hard constraints are 
transformed into dynamic selection pressures: 
a. Connectivity Handling: Quickly determine connectivity based on graph theory 
search, using “main-component anchoring + incremental component connection” re-
pairs, with a preference for low-cost lines. 
b. N-1 Connectivity Assessment: Abstract the network as a unit -capacity undirected 
graph, with core loads as sources and pumped-storage as sinks, calculating edge con-
nectivity using the max -flow min-cut theorem to identify key reinforcement edges 
that guide evolution. 
c. Power Flow Safety Check: In Stage III, individuals that meet connectivity and N -1 
connectivity constraints undergo dual -scenario DC power flow calculations. A uni-
fied assessment is performed using dual-scenario (generation/pumping) risk indices 
𝑅total, with only individuals meeting safety standards retained. The risk indices pro-
vide a continuous search gradient, thereby avoiding the “cliff effect” caused by bi-
nary feasibility judgments.

sections.title: 5.3 Periodic Reverse Learning Mechanism
sections.text:
To further enhance the global search capability of TER-NSGA-II in discrete backbone-
grid planning problems, a periodic reverse learning mechanism is introduced. The core 
idea is that, after several generations of evolution, part of the population may become 
clustered within a limited search region. If only conventional crossover and mutation op-
erators are applied, the search process tends to remain confined to the current neighbor-
hood, leading to reduced population diversity and an increased risk of premature conver-
gence. Therefore, reverse learning is triggered every 𝑇𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑒 generations. By constructing 
reverse individuals with complementary line -selection patterns relative to the original 
Energies 2026, 19, 2798 10 of 26 
 
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19122798 
solutions, the search space is actively expanded, providing additional candidate solutions 
for subsequent environmental selection. 
For any individual, its chromosome is defined as the binary decision vector 𝒀 in (9), 
where 𝑦𝑖 = 1 indicates that candidate line i is selected into the backbone grid, and 𝑦𝑖 = 0 
otherwise. Reverse learning is implemented by performing a bitwise inversion on this bi-
nary structure. Given an original individual 𝒀, its reverse individual is defined as 𝒀 =
𝟏 − 𝒀, i.e., 𝑦𝑖̅ = 1 − 𝑦𝑖. This operation implies that the lines retained in the original solu-
tion are preferentially removed in the reversed solution, while the unselected lines are 
activated. As a result, the reverse individual is able to escape from the local structural 
pattern of the original solution and generate a new topology significantly different from 
the current population. 
As illustrated in Figure 1, a simplified example is used to demonstrate the structural 
transformation of a reverse chromosome before and after connectivity repair. Since a fea-
sible solution must ensure that key nodes are connected to the backbone grid, consider an 
individual with chromosome 𝒀, where selected candidate lines form a topology that sat-
isfies the key-node connectivity requirement. After applying bitwise inversion, the reverse 
chromosome 𝒀 is obtained. Due to the drastic change in line combinations, the reversed 
topology may violate connectivity constraints, potentially resulting in network disconnec-
tion or isolation of key nodes. Therefore, it cannot directly participate in environmental 
selection. 
To address this issue, a connectivity repair procedure is first applied to the reversed 
individual. By adding necessary critical lines, the network is restored to a connected state. 
Let the repaired individual be denoted as  𝒀𝑟𝑒𝑝, whose corresponding topology satisfies 
the connectivity requirement and can proceed to subsequent selection.  
It should be noted that connectivity repair is only the first step for reintroducing re-
verse individuals into the candidate solution set. Based on the current evolutionary stage, 
additional constraint handling is performed. Specifically, in Stage II, furth er reinforce-
ment of N-1 connectivity is conducted, while in Stage III, dual -scenario power flow secu-
rity constraints are evaluated. In other words, reverse learning introduces complementary 
search directions rather than directly producing feasible solutions. Its effectiveness lies in 
the combined process of “reverse generation + constraint repair + environmental selec-
tion,” which introduces structurally diverse yet potentially feasible candidate solutions 
into the population. 
From a procedural perspective, the periodic reverse learning mechanism can be sum-
marized into five steps: 
a. Reverse learning is triggered when the current generation satisfies 𝑡 𝑚𝑜𝑑 𝑇reverse = 0; 
b. Each individual in the population undergoes bitwise inversion to generate reverse 
chromosomes; 
c. Connectivity repair is first applied, followed by stage -dependent constraint han-
dling; 
d. The repaired reverse individuals are merged with the original population and off-
spring solutions to form an expanded candidate set; 
e. Non-dominated sorting, crowding distance calculation, and elite preservation are 
performed to select individuals for the next generation. 
Therefore, periodic reverse learning is not a simple random perturbation, but a mech-
anism that constructs complementary search directions based on existing high-quality so-
lutions. Through constraint repair and environmental selection, only promising solutions 
are retained. This mechanism expands the search space while maintaining solution qual-
ity, effectively reducing the risk of stagnation in local optima without disrupting the over-
all evolutionary framework of TER-NSGA-II.

sections.title: 5.5 Theoretical Performance Analysis of the Algorithm
sections.text:
The three-stage iterative framework activates constraints in layers, encouraging the 
population to gradually satisfy stricter engineering requirements and improving the fea-
sible-domain search tendency.  Let the proportion of individuals in the 𝑡-th generation 
satisfying the stage 𝑠 constraint be denoted as 𝑝𝑠(𝑡). Stage I only requires connectivity 
constraints, so its feasible solution space ℱ1 is much larger than that of Stage II (ℱ2, which 
requires N-1 connectivity), and Stage III has the smallest feasible solution space ℱ3(which 
additionally requires power flow safety). Since the elite selection strategy preferentially 
retains individuals with low constraint violation values, and repair operations are guided 
in each generation, the following tendency can be expected: 
𝑝1(𝑡 + 1) ≥ 𝑝1(𝑡), 𝑝2(𝑡 + 1) ≥ 𝑝2(𝑡) (26) 
When switching between stages, the feasible solutions accumulated in the previous 
stage provide a high -quality initial population for the next stage, so the overall feasible -
solution probability is expected to improve as the evolutionary process proceeds.  In the 
IEEE 118-bus experiments, TER -NSGA-II achieved a 100.00% feasible -run rate across all 
independent runs, whereas NSGA -II achieved only 48.11%. This result is consistent with 
the above theoretical analysis. 
The main computational cost of TER -NSGA-II comes from non -dominated sorting, 
constraint validation, and reverse learning. Let the population size be 𝑀, the maximum 
number of generations be 𝑇𝑚𝑎𝑥, and the number of candidate lines be 𝐻(𝐻 = |𝐸|). The 
time complexity of non-dominated sorting is 𝑂(𝑀2), and connectivity and N-1 connectiv-
ity validation for each pair of core -load and pumped-storage buses requires the Dinic al-
gorithm, which has a complexity of 𝑂(𝑚𝑖𝑛( 𝑉2/3, 𝐻1/2)𝐸). Given that in the IEEE 118-bus 
system, only 10 bus pairs need to be calculated, this part is actually much less time -con-
suming than non-dominated sorting. Therefore, the total time complexity is 𝑂(𝑇𝑚𝑎𝑥𝑀2 +
𝑇𝑚𝑎𝑥𝑀𝐻), which is higher than the standard NSGA-II’s 𝑂(𝑇𝑚𝑎𝑥𝑀2), but due to the signif-
icant improvement in feasible solution rates, the algorithm avoids a large amount of re-
dundant search. Under the same number of iterations, the probability of obtaining feasible 
high-quality solutions is therefore improved relative to that of traditional methods.

sections.title: 6.1 Test Systems and Experimental Settings
sections.text:
The IEEE 118 -bus system is employed as the main test system  to validate the pro-
posed planning approach.  The system configuration includes core generation buses 
(Buses 10, 69, 80, and 89), core -load buses (Buses 11, 16, 20, 29, and 50), and PSH units 
used as black-start resources (Buses 63 and 64, each with 240 MW).  The planning model 
is subject to the N -1 connectivity constraint, which strictly requires an edge connectivity 
of 𝜆 ≥ 2 between critical load centers and black -start units, together with dual -scenario 
steady-state security requirements. 
Energies 2026, 19, 2798 14 of 26 
 
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19122798 
To further examine the scalability of the proposed method, an additional IEEE 300 -
bus system is used for extended validation under the same modeling framework. This 
extended case is intended to assess the applicability of the proposed method to larger -
scale networks and to examine whether the algorithm can maintain acceptable optimiza-
tion performance as network size increases. 
For TER-NSGA-II, the population size is set to 50 and the maximum number of gen-
erations is set to 200 in the IEEE 118-bus case. The stage-related parameters are determined 
through the irace-based tuning procedure described in Section 6.2, and the final con figu-
ration is set to 𝑇1 = 77, 𝑇2 = 115, and 𝑇reverse = 49. 
To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, NSGA-II and the more re-
cent reference-point-based algorithm NSGA -III/NG are adopted as benchmark methods 
[42]. All compared algorithms use the same decision encoding, population size, termina-
tion criterion, network data, and constraint -evaluation criteria, so that the comparison is 
conducted under a unified problem definition and a consistent feasible-domain criterion.

sections.title: 6.2 Parameter Tuning and Configuration of TER-NSGA-II
sections.text:
To avoid relying entirely on empirical parameter settings, the key stage -related pa-
rameters of TER -NSGA-II are tuned using irace, an automatic algorithm -configuration 
procedure. Since 𝑇1, 𝑇2, and 𝑇reverse are all scale-dependent with respect to the total num-
ber of generations 𝐺, they are first rewritten in normalized ratio form as 𝑝1 = 𝑇1/𝐺, 𝑝2 =
𝑇2/𝐺, and 𝑝𝑟 = 𝑇reverse/𝐺. This ratio-based formulation allows the tuned configuration to 
better reflect the relative allocation of search effort across the three evolutionary stages.  
During the tuning process, two aspects are considered simultaneously: the ability to 
generate feasible solutions under strong constraints and the overall bi-objective optimiza-
tion performance. Several representative candidate configurations are screened and com-
pared. As summarized in Table 1, the Baseline corresponds to the original empirical set-
ting, whereas Candidate A, Candidate B, and Candidate C are representative configura-
tions selected during the automatic tuning process. Although some candidates ach ieve 
lower scalarized tuning costs, they may still exhibit high zero-cost frequency, small feasi-
ble-solution-set size, or unstable performance across repeated runs. Therefore, the final 
parameter setting is selected not only according to the mean tuning cost, but also accord-
ing to feasible-solution generation capability and run-to-run stability.
